transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Park, thank you for meeting with me. I wanted to sit down and talk to you about what happened during your chemotherapy infusion yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, okay. Is it about the vomiting?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, it is. I want to be very direct with you. We made a mistake. The anti-nausea medication that was supposed to be part of your pre-treatment orders was not added to the list. Because of that, you didn't receive the medicine that prevents nausea, which is why you became so sick during the infusion. I am very sorry for this. This was our error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh. I just thought maybe I was just reacting bad to the chemo.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a common side effect, but in this case, it was preventable. You should have had that medication in your system before we started. Does that make sense, or can I explain that differently?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I think I get it. It's just... it was really scary. I've never been in a hospital alone before.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can imagine how overwhelming that felt, especially being here on your own without your parents. It's a lot to handle.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. I just didn't want to be a bother, so I didn't even tell the nurse I felt weird until I actually started throwing up.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I appreciate you telling me that. It sounds like you were trying to be patient and not cause a scene, but you shouldn't have had to push through that feeling. Does that sound right?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess. Is this going to happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be honest with you. We are still investigating exactly how the medication was missed in the computer system so we can make sure it doesn't happen again. I don't have the final answer on the "how" yet, but I can promise you that for your next visit, we are changing the process. I will personally double-check the pre-medication list with the pharmacy and the nursing lead forty-eight hours before you arrive. We are also adding a mandatory "stop-gap" check in the electronic chart that requires two different clinicians to sign off on the nausea meds before the infusion begins.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I didn't know there was a process for that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There is, and it failed yesterday. That's on us. Just to make sure I've been clear, what is your understanding of why you got sick yesterday?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That you guys forgot the medicine that stops the nausea.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's correct. I'm sorry we put you through that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's okay. I mean, I'm not mad. I just... I don't really know if I'm supposed to do anything about this? Like, is there a form?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You have every right to ask for a formal incident report. I've already started the internal report, but I can provide you with a copy of the summary once the investigation is closed, which should be by next Friday. I'll email that to you directly. In the meantime, I want you to be my eyes and ears. If you feel even a hint of nausea during the next round, I want you to tell the nurse immediately. Please don't worry about being a bother. Your comfort is the priority. Does that sound like a plan you're okay with?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah, I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know we've covered a lot, and I have to get to my next patient in a second, so if there's anything else, just let me know quickly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Um, will my parents find out? I haven't told them the full story.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can respect your privacy here. Since you're an adult, I won't share this with them unless you want me to. But if you do decide to tell them and they have questions, I'm happy to get on a call with them to explain exactly what happened and how we're fixing it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thanks. I think I'm okay for now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Okay. I'll send you a follow-up message today with my direct number and the date of our next check-in. I'll see you soon.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language at the end of the encounter ('I have to get to my next patient in a second, so if there's anything else, just let me know quickly').

E.justification: The error was named in the first turn, lay language was used, and comprehension was checked twice ('Does that make sense...?' and 'what is your understanding...?').

A.justification: The resident used direct apology language ('I am very sorry') and explicitly took responsibility ('This was our error', 'That's on us').

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('overwhelming', 'trying to be patient') and engaged with the patient's shared experience of being alone in the hospital.

T.justification: The resident provided specific prevention steps, a timeline for the report (next Friday), and a named role for the patient ('be my eyes and ears').
